claim: Epithelial cells adhere tightly to their apical neighbours in a virtually impermeable adhesion belt.
source: Characterised by apical-basal polarity (Figure 1a), epithelial cells adhere tightly to their apical neighbours in a virtually impermeable adhesion belt, form lateral cell-cell junction complexes along the apico-basal axis to provide mechanical stabilisation, and bind tightly to the basal lamina and extracellular matrix (ECM) on the basal side (Drubin and Nelson, 1996; Rodriguez-Boulan and Macara, 2014; Shin and Margolis, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Drubin and Nelson, 1996; Rodriguez-Boulan and Macara, 2014; Shin and Margolis, 2006).

claim: Epithelial cells form lateral cell-cell junction complexes along the apico-basal axis to provide mechanical stabilisation.
source: Characterised by apical-basal polarity (Figure 1a), epithelial cells adhere tightly to their apical neighbours in a virtually impermeable adhesion belt, form lateral cell-cell junction complexes along the apico-basal axis to provide mechanical stabilisation, and bind tightly to the basal lamina and extracellular matrix (ECM) on the basal side (Drubin and Nelson, 1996; Rodriguez-Boulan and Macara, 2014; Shin and Margolis, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Drubin and Nelson, 1996; Rodriguez-Boulan and Macara, 2014; Shin and Margolis, 2006).

claim: Epithelial cells bind tightly to the basal lamina and extracellular matrix (ECM) on the basal side.
source: Characterised by apical-basal polarity (Figure 1a), epithelial cells adhere tightly to their apical neighbours in a virtually impermeable adhesion belt, form lateral cell-cell junction complexes along the apico-basal axis to provide mechanical stabilisation, and bind tightly to the basal lamina and extracellular matrix (ECM) on the basal side (Drubin and Nelson, 1996; Rodriguez-Boulan and Macara, 2014; Shin and Margolis, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Drubin and Nelson, 1996; Rodriguez-Boulan and Macara, 2014; Shin and Margolis, 2006).

claim: Cells have on average (close to) six neighbours in epithelial tissues.
source: First, even though the frequencies of neighbour numbers differ widely between epithelial tissues (Figure 1e), cells have on average (close to) six neighbours (Classen et al., 2005; Escudero et al., 2011; Etournay et al., 2015; Farhadifar et al., 2007; Gibson et al., 2006; Heller et al., 2016; Kokic et al., 2019; Ramanathan et al., 2019; Sánchez-Gutiérrez et al., 2016; Figure 1f).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature and reference to Figure 1f showing data.

claim: Aboav-Weaire's law and Lewis' law are a direct consequence of a minimisation of the lateral cell-cell contact surface energy.
source: We have recently shown that Aboav-Weaire's law and Lewis' law are a direct consequence of a minimisation of the lateral cell-cell contact surface energy (Kokic et al., 2019; Vetter et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to authors' prior work (Kokic et al., 2019; Vetter et al., 2019).

claim: The lowest lateral cell-cell contact surface energy is obtained in a regular polygonal lattice because regular polygons have the smallest perimeter per polygonal area.
source: The lowest lateral cell-cell contact surface energy is obtained in a regular polygonal lattice because regular polygons have the smallest perimeter per polygonal area.
evidence: Based on geometric principles and physical reasoning.

claim: Cells in embryonic lung epithelia have highly irregular 3D shapes.
source: We find that cells have highly irregular 3D shapes and exhibit numerous neighbour intercalations along the apical-basal axis as well as over time.
evidence: Stated as a finding from the study's observations.

claim: Cells exhibit numerous neighbour intercalations along the apical-basal axis as well as over time.
source: We find that cells have highly irregular 3D shapes and exhibit numerous neighbour intercalations along the apical-basal axis as well as over time.
evidence: Stated as a finding from the study's observations.

claim: Cell packing configurations follow Euler's polyhedron formula at all times and across the entire tissue thickness.
source: Despite the fluidic nature, the cell packing configurations follow fundamental relationships previously described for apical epithelial layers, that is, Euler's polyhedron formula, Lewis' law, and Aboav-Weaire's law, at all times and across the entire tissue thickness.
evidence: Stated as a finding from the study's observations.

claim: Cell packing configurations follow Lewis' law at all times and across the entire tissue thickness.
source: Despite the fluidic nature, the cell packing configurations follow fundamental relationships previously described for apical epithelial layers, that is, Euler's polyhedron formula, Lewis' law, and Aboav-Weaire's law, at all times and across the entire tissue thickness.
evidence: Stated as a finding from the study's observations.

claim: Cell packing configurations follow Aboav-Weaire's law at all times and across the entire tissue thickness.
source: Despite the fluidic nature, the cell packing configurations follow fundamental relationships previously described for apical epithelial layers, that is, Euler's polyhedron formula, Lewis' law, and Aboav-Weaire's law, at all times and across the entire tissue thickness.
evidence: Stated as a finding from the study's observations.

claim: The cell arrangement minimises the lateral cell-cell surface energy for a given cross-sectional area variability.
source: This arrangement minimises the lateral cell-cell surface energy for a given cross-sectional area variability, generated primarily by the distribution and movement of nuclei.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the study's observations and theoretical framework.

claim: Cross-sectional area variability is generated primarily by the distribution and movement of nuclei.
source: This arrangement minimises the lateral cell-cell surface energy for a given cross-sectional area variability, generated primarily by the distribution and movement of nuclei.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the study's observations.

claim: The complex 3D cell organisation in growing epithelia emerges from simple physical principles.
source: We conclude that the complex 3D cell organisation in growing epithelia emerges from simple physical principles.
evidence: Stated as the main conclusion of the study.

claim: The total segmented apical area is about 5-fold smaller than the basal area in embryonic lung epithelia.
source: The apical and basal surfaces are both curved and thus differ in their total areas, that is, the total segmented apical area is about 5-fold smaller than the basal area (Figure 2b).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Less than half as many cells are detected on the apical side compared to the basal side in embryonic lung epithelia.
source: We detected less than half as many cells on the apical side, and the mean cross-sectional cell area of apical cells is therefore on average only twofold smaller than that of basal cells, while the area variability, measured as area CV, is higher (Figure 2c).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The mean cross-sectional cell area of apical cells is on average only twofold smaller than that of basal cells.
source: We detected less than half as many cells on the apical side, and the mean cross-sectional cell area of apical cells is therefore on average only twofold smaller than that of basal cells, while the area variability, measured as area CV, is higher (Figure 2c).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The area variability is higher on the apical side than the basal side.
source: We detected less than half as many cells on the apical side, and the mean cross-sectional cell area of apical cells is therefore on average only twofold smaller than that of basal cells, while the area variability, measured as area CV, is higher (Figure 2c).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The frequencies of the different neighbour numbers are not identical on the apical and basal side.
source: Notably, the frequencies of the different neighbour numbers are not identical on the apical and basal side (Figure 2d), suggesting that the neighbour relationships change along the apical-basal axis, both in the tube and tip datasets.

claim: Neighbour relationships change along the apical-basal axis in both tube and tip datasets.

claim: The apical and basal layers follow Aboav-Weaire's law.
source: We now find that these hold not only for the apical, but also for the basal datasets (Figure 2e,f).
evidence: Stated as a finding from the study's observations shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Apical layers with larger area variability follow the quadratic law rather than the linear Lewis' law.
source: Consistent with our theory, the apical layers, which have a larger area variability than the basal layers (Figure 2c), follow the quadratic law (yellow line) rather than the linear Lewis' law (black line).
evidence: Stated as a finding from the study's observations shown in Figure 2f.

claim: Basal layers follow the same organisational principles as apical layers.
source: We conclude that basal layers follow the same organisational principles as apical layers, such that their organisation can also be explained with a minimisation of the lateral cell-cell contact surface energy.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the study's observations.

claim: The 3D organisation of epithelial cells is highly complex.
source: In both datasets, the 3D organisation of epithelial cells is highly complex, and cell neighbour relationships change continuously along the apical-basal axis (Figure 3b).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Cell neighbour relationships change continuously along the apical-basal axis.
source: In both datasets, the 3D organisation of epithelial cells is highly complex, and cell neighbour relationships change continuously along the apical-basal axis (Figure 3b).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Cells are in direct physical contact with cells that appear two or even three cell diameters apart on the apical side.
source: As a result, cells are in direct physical contact not only with the cells that are neighbours on the apical side, but also with cells that appear two or even three cell diameters apart (Figure 3c).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Cells record up to 14 cell neighbour changes per cell in the tube between adjacent cross-sections along the apical-basal cell axis.
source: Remarkably, we record up to 14 cell neighbour changes per cell in the tube and up to eight in the tip, between adjacent cross-sections along the apical-basal cell axis (Figure 3d).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Cells record up to eight cell neighbour changes per cell in the tip between adjacent cross-sections along the apical-basal cell axis.
source: Remarkably, we record up to 14 cell neighbour changes per cell in the tube and up to eight in the tip, between adjacent cross-sections along the apical-basal cell axis (Figure 3d).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The mean relative apical-basal position for lateral T1 transitions is 0.489±0.020 (95% CI).
source: The mean relative apical-basal position for the lateral T1 transitions is 0.489±0.020 (95% CI), and there is no clear apical or basal tendency, though fewer transitions are observed close to the basal surface (Figure 3e).
evidence: Stated as a quantitative observation from the data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: There is no clear apical or basal tendency for lateral T1 transitions, though fewer transitions are observed close to the basal surface.
source: The mean relative apical-basal position for the lateral T1 transitions is 0.489±0.020 (95% CI), and there is no clear apical or basal tendency, though fewer transitions are observed close to the basal surface (Figure 3e).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: The number of apical-basal T1 transitions per cell is Poisson-distributed.
source: The chi-squared test also confirms that the number of apical-basal T1 transitions per cell is Poisson-distributed (Figure 3d).
evidence: Stated as a finding from statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The consistency with a Poisson distribution suggests a stochastic basis to the 3D organisation of epithelial cells.
source: A Poisson distribution models the probability of a number of independent random events occurring in a given interval at a constant average rate. The consistency with a Poisson distribution, therefore, suggests a stochastic basis to the 3D organisation of epithelial cells.
evidence: Inferred from the statistical properties of the data.

claim: The mean apical-basal distance between two consecutive neighbour number changes is 17.89 ± 0.66 µm (95% CI).
source: The mean apical-basal distance between two transitions is 17.89 ± 0.66 µm (95% CI).
evidence: Stated as a quantitative observation from the data.

claim: The examined tissue exhibits an average curvature fold change of R(1)/R(0)=2.21 from the basal to the apical side.
source: The examined tissue exhibits an average curvature fold change of R(1)/R(0)=2.21 from the basal to the apical side.
evidence: Stated as a quantitative observation from the data.

claim: The mean curvature fold change per apical-basal T1L transition per cell is <R2/R1> = 1.142 ± 0.010 (95% CI).
source: The mean curvature fold change per apical-basal T1L transition per cell is <R2/R1> = 1.142 ± 0.010 (95% CI).
evidence: Stated as a quantitative observation from the data.

claim: There is no systematic dependency of the curvature fold change on the number of neighbours the cell has along that portion of the cell in the developing mouse lung epithelium.
source: However, we observe no systematic dependency of the curvature fold change on the number of neighbours the cell has along that portion of the cell in the developing mouse lung epithelium (Figure 3g).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 3g.

claim: Tissue curvature affects cell neighbourhood rearrangements through the tissue thickness at most mildly.
source: From this, we conclude that tissue curvature affects cell neighbourhood rearrangements through the tissue thickness at most mildly.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the study's observations.

claim: Each layer along the apical-basal axis behaves according to Euler's polyhedron formula.
source: We notice that much as the apical and basal layers, each layer along the apical-basal axis behaves according to the three relationships previously described for the apical side, that is, Euler's polyhedron formula (Equation 1, Figure 4a), Aboav-Weaire's law (Equation 2, Figure 4b), and Lewis' law (Equations 3, 4, Figure 4c).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Each layer along the apical-basal axis behaves according to Aboav-Weaire's law.
source: We notice that much as the apical and basal layers, each layer along the apical-basal axis behaves according to the three relationships previously described for the apical side, that is, Euler's polyhedron formula (Equation 1, Figure 4a), Aboav-Weaire's law (Equation 2, Figure 4b), and Lewis' law (Equations 3, 4, Figure 4c).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Each layer along the apical-basal axis behaves according to Lewis' law.
source: We notice that much as the apical and basal layers, each layer along the apical-basal axis behaves according to the three relationships previously described for the apical side, that is, Euler's polyhedron formula (Equation 1, Figure 4a), Aboav-Weaire's law (Equation 2, Figure 4b), and Lewis' law (Equations 3, 4, Figure 4c).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Layers with large area variability follow the quadratic law.
source: As predicted by the theory based on the minimisation of the lateral cell-cell energy (Kokic et al., 2019), the layers with a large area variability (Figure 4a) follow the quadratic law (yellow line) and those with a lower area variability the linear Lewis' law (black line).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Layers with lower area variability follow the linear Lewis' law.
source: As predicted by the theory based on the minimisation of the lateral cell-cell energy (Kokic et al., 2019), the layers with a large area variability (Figure 4a) follow the quadratic law (yellow line) and those with a lower area variability the linear Lewis' law (black line).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The fraction of hexagons follows the predicted relationship with the cross-sectional area variability.
source: The fraction of hexagons also follows the predicted relationship with the cross-sectional area variability (Figure 4d).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The neighbour relationships of epithelial cells along the entire apical-basal axis can be explained with a minimisation of the lateral cell-cell contact surface energy.
source: We conclude that the neighbour relationships of epithelial cells along the entire apical-basal axis can be explained with a minimisation of the lateral cell-cell contact surface energy, as previously revealed for the apical layer.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the study's observations.

claim: An increase in the cross-sectional area results in an increase in the neighbour number.
source: If we analyse four 3D segmented cells (Figure 4e) in detail, we indeed see how an increase in the cross-sectional area results in an increase in the neighbour number, and vice versa (Figure 4f) via lateral T1 transitions (Figure 4g).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figures 4e-g.

claim: The frequency of T1L transitions along the apical-basal axis is higher, the larger the increase in cross-sectional area.
source: When we consider all 140 segmented cells in the tube segment with their 746 cell neighbour exchanges between adjacent cross-sections (Figure 3e), then we find that the frequency of T1L transitions along the apical-basal axis is indeed higher, the larger the increase in cross-sectional area, and vice versa (Figure 4h,i).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figures 4h,i.

claim: In pseudostratified epithelia, mitosis is restricted to the apical surface.
source: In pseudostratified epithelia, mitosis is restricted to the apical surface (Gundersen and Worman, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Gundersen and Worman, 2013).

claim: As a cell exits mitosis, the nucleus moves from the apical towards the basal side (G1 and S phase) and then back to the apical side (G2 phase) to undergo another round of mitosis.
source: Therefore, as a cell exits mitosis, the nucleus moves from the apical towards the basal side (G1 and S phase) and then back to the apical side (G2 phase) to undergo another round of mitosis, a process referred to as interkinetic nuclear migration (IKNM) (Meyer et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Meyer et al., 2011).

claim: Nuclei are distributed along the entire apical-basal axis in pseudostratified epithelia.
source: The nuclei were distributed along the entire apical-basal axis (Figure 5c), and consistent with the pseudostratified appearance of the epithelium, nuclei in neighbouring cells had different positions along the apical-basal axis (Figure 5b).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figures 5b,c.

claim: Nuclei in neighbouring cells have different positions along the apical-basal axis.
source: The nuclei were distributed along the entire apical-basal axis (Figure 5c), and consistent with the pseudostratified appearance of the epithelium, nuclei in neighbouring cells had different positions along the apical-basal axis (Figure 5b).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Nuclei are largest and most spherical at the apical side, where they undergo mitosis.
source: As expected, nuclei are largest and most spherical at the apical side, where they undergo mitosis (Figure 5d).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Nuclei located in the first 25% of the apical-basal axis have significantly reduced ellipticity compared to those in the middle 50%.
source: Thus, a one-sided, two-sample Welch t-test revealed a significantly reduced ellipticity of nuclei located in the first 25% of the apical-basal axis compared to those in the middle 50% (p=0.0002).
evidence: Stated as a finding from statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Nuclear volumes are on average about 50% smaller than the cell volumes.
source: The nuclear volumes are on average about 50% smaller than the cell volumes and largely correlate (r = 0.79, Figure 5f), likely reflecting parallel expansion during the cell cycle.
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 5f.

claim: Nuclear volumes and cell volumes largely correlate (r = 0.79).
source: The nuclear volumes are on average about 50% smaller than the cell volumes and largely correlate (r = 0.79, Figure 5f), likely reflecting parallel expansion during the cell cycle.
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 5f.

claim: The cross-sectional areas of the cell and the nucleus are strongly correlated (r = 0.94).
source: Where present, the nuclear cross-sectional areas are only slightly smaller than those of the entire cell, and the cross-sectional areas of the cell and the nucleus are strongly correlated (r = 0.94, Figure 5g).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 5g.

claim: The nuclear volumes are too large to allow for a spherical nucleus to fit into a cylindrical cell of the measured height.
source: The nuclear volumes are too large to allow for a spherical nucleus to fit into a cylindrical cell of the measured height (Figure 5h).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 5h.

claim: To fit into the cell, the nucleus necessarily has to deform.
source: Accordingly, to fit into the cell, the nucleus necessarily has to deform.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that nuclear volumes are too large to fit as spheres.

claim: Nuclei respond to external forces with anisotropic shape changes.
source: Nuclei respond to external forces with anisotropic shape changes (Haase et al., 2016; Neelam et al., 2016), which is consistent with the elliptical nuclear shapes that we observe (Figure 5d).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Haase et al., 2016; Neelam et al., 2016) and observation in Figure 5d.

claim: There is a limit to how much the stiff nucleus can deform.
source: However, there is a limit to how much the stiff nucleus can deform (Lammerding, 2011; Shah et al., 2021), resulting in a local widening of the cell where the nucleus is present.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Lammerding, 2011; Shah et al., 2021).

claim: The stiff nucleus results in a local widening of the cell where the nucleus is present.
source: However, there is a limit to how much the stiff nucleus can deform (Lammerding, 2011; Shah et al., 2021), resulting in a local widening of the cell where the nucleus is present.
evidence: Inferred from the physical properties of the nucleus and observations.

claim: Most T1L transitions occur where the nucleus starts and ends.
source: Accordingly, as previously seen for the cell cross-sectional areas, the observed changes in cell neighbour numbers correlates with the observed changes in nuclear cross-sectional areas (Figure 5i) such that most T1L transitions occur where the nucleus starts and ends (Figure 5j).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figures 5i,j.

claim: The positions of nuclei can explain much of the observed variability in the cross-sectional cell areas.
source: We conclude that the positions of nuclei can explain much of the observed variability in the cross-sectional cell areas.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the study's observations.

claim: During the cell cycle, nuclei migrate, and the cell volumes first increase, and subsequently halve due to cell division.
source: During the cell cycle, nuclei migrate, and the cell volumes first increase, and subsequently halve due to cell division.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of cell cycle processes.

claim: All processes that affect the cross-sectional areas of the cells along the apical-basal axis would be expected to result in continuous spatial-temporal T1L transitions in growing pseudostratified epithelia.
source: As all these processes affect the cross-sectional areas of the cells along the apical-basal axis, one would expect continuous spatial-temporal T1L transitions in growing pseudostratified epithelia.
evidence: Inferred from the relationship between cross-sectional area changes and T1L transitions.

claim: For all time points, both the apical and basal layers conformed to Euler's polyhedron formula.
source: However, for all time points, both the apical and basal layers conformed to Euler's polyhedron formula (Figure 6c), Aboav-Weaire's law (Figure 6d), and Lewis' law (Figure 6e).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: For all time points, both the apical and basal layers conformed to Aboav-Weaire's law.
source: However, for all time points, both the apical and basal layers conformed to Euler's polyhedron formula (Figure 6c), Aboav-Weaire's law (Figure 6d), and Lewis' law (Figure 6e).

claim: For all time points, both the apical and basal layers conformed to Lewis' law.
source: However, for all time points, both the apical and basal layers conformed to Euler's polyhedron formula (Figure 6c), Aboav-Weaire's law (Figure 6d), and Lewis' law (Figure 6e).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 6e.

claim: The fraction of hexagons follows from the variability of the cross-sectional areas, as predicted by the theory.
source: Furthermore, the fraction of hexagons also followed from the variability of the cross-sectional areas, as predicted by the theory (Figure 6f).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 6f.

claim: The volume of individual cells varied between roughly 400 and 800 µm3 over the time course.
source: Over the time course, the volume of individual cells varied between roughly 400 and 800 µm3 (Figure 7b), and the apical-basal length varied between roughly 20 and 30 µm (Figure 7c).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: The apical-basal length of cells varied between roughly 20 and 30 µm over the time course.
source: Over the time course, the volume of individual cells varied between roughly 400 and 800 µm3 (Figure 7b), and the apical-basal length varied between roughly 20 and 30 µm (Figure 7c).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 7c.

claim: All layers conform to Aboav-Weaire's law in all time points.
source: We note that all layers conform to Aboav-Weaire's law (Figure 7d) and Lewis' law (Figure 7e) in all time points.
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 7d.

claim: All layers conform to Lewis' law in all time points.
source: We note that all layers conform to Aboav-Weaire's law (Figure 7d) and Lewis' law (Figure 7e) in all time points.
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 7e.

claim: The fraction of hexagons follows from the variability of the cross-sectional area in the time-lapse dataset.
source: Moreover, consistent with our theory, the fraction of hexagons follows from the variability of the cross-sectional area, though more deviations are observed, given the small number of cells analysed (Figure 7f).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 7f.

claim: Up to 14 neighbour number changes (T1L transitions) are observed along the apical-basal axis in the time-lapse dataset.
source: Much as in the static dataset (Figures 3 and 4), we observe up to 14 neighbour number changes (T1L transitions) along the apical-basal axis (Figure 8a,b).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figures 8a,b.

claim: The average number of T1L transitions is relatively constant over time.
source: The average number of T1L transitions is relatively constant over time (Figure 8b).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 8b.

claim: A change in the cross-sectional area correlates with a change in neighbour number in single cells over time.
source: By following a single cell over time, we can appreciate the dynamic cell shape changes, and how a change in the cross-sectional area correlates with a change in neighbour number (Figure 8d).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 8d.

claim: Pseudostratified epithelial layers adopt a far more complex packing solution than previously anticipated.
source: Our analysis reveals that pseudostratified epithelial layers adopt a far more complex packing solution than previously anticipated: the 3D epithelial cell shapes are highly irregular, and cell neighbour relationships change multiple times along the apical-basal axis, with some cells having up to 14 changes in their neighbour contacts along their apical-basal axis (Figure 3a).
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the study's observations.

claim: Some cells have up to 14 changes in their neighbour contacts along their apical-basal axis.
source: Our analysis reveals that pseudostratified epithelial layers adopt a far more complex packing solution than previously anticipated: the 3D epithelial cell shapes are highly irregular, and cell neighbour relationships change multiple times along the apical-basal axis, with some cells having up to 14 changes in their neighbour contacts along their apical-basal axis (Figure 3a).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The data does not show the dependency on cell neighbour numbers that would be expected if curvature effects played a dominating role.
source: Curvature effects can result in neighbour changes, but the data does not show the dependency on cell neighbour numbers that would be expected if curvature effects played a dominating role (Figure 3g).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 3g.

claim: The prevalence of contact remodelling is randomly distributed.
source: There is also no apical-basal bias (Figure 3e), and the prevalence of contact remodelling is randomly distributed (Figure 4i).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 4i.

claim: Neighbour relationships in epithelia are fluidic.
source: We conclude that neighbour relationships in epithelia are fluidic, and the complex, dynamic 3D organisation of cells in growing epithelia follows simple physical principles.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the study's observations.

claim: The complex, dynamic 3D organisation of cells in growing epithelia follows simple physical principles.
source: We conclude that neighbour relationships in epithelia are fluidic, and the complex, dynamic 3D organisation of cells in growing epithelia follows simple physical principles.
evidence: Stated as the main conclusion of the study.

claim: The nucleus occupies, on average, 55% of the cell volume in the embryonic lung epithelia.
source: We find that the nucleus occupies, on average, 55% of the cell volume in the embryonic lung epithelia.
evidence: Stated as a quantitative observation from the data.

claim: As the cell nuclei move along the apical-basal axis during the cell cycle, the cytoplasm fills the remaining space between the apical and basal surfaces, likely in a way that minimises the total surface area of all cells.
source: As the cell nuclei move along the apical-basal axis during the cell cycle (Meyer et al., 2011), the cytoplasm fills the remaining space between the apical and basal surfaces, likely in a way that minimises the total surface area of all cells.
evidence: Inferred from observations and physical principles, with citation to prior literature (Meyer et al., 2011).

claim: Signalling downstream of FGF, SHH, BMP/TGF-β, and WNT has been observed to affect cell height.
source: The determinants of the epithelial thickness, that is, the distance between the apical and basal surfaces are still unknown, but signalling downstream of Fibroblastic Growth Factor (FGF), Sonic Hedgehog (SHH), Bone Morphogenetic Protein (BMP)/ transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β), and WNT has been observed to affect cell height, presumably via an effect on cell tension and/or cell-cell adhesion (Gritli-Linde et al., 2002; Hirashima and Matsuda, 2021; Kadzik et al., 2014; Kondo and Hayashi, 2015; Widmann and Dahmann, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Gritli-Linde et al., 2002; Hirashima and Matsuda, 2021; Kadzik et al., 2014; Kondo and Hayashi, 2015; Widmann and Dahmann, 2009).

claim: Signalling downstream of FGF, SHH, BMP/TGF-β, and WNT presumably affects cell height via an effect on cell tension and/or cell-cell adhesion.
